newsitem.title: USA: FAA orders rudder modifications of Boeing 737s.
newsitem.headline: FAA orders rudder modifications of Boeing 737s.

text.p: Federal aviation authorities Friday ordered airlines flying the Boeing Co. 737 to make a series of modifications to correct unsafe conditions in the popular plane's rudder controls.

The Federal Aviation Administration airworthiness directive (AD) stemmed from recommendations by a design review team formed after two incidents in which 737s went into uncontrolled rolls and crashed, killing a total of 157 people.
One comment received on the proposed directive suggested the agency remove a sentence saying the review called for corrections of "certain design deficiencies," but the FAA rejected this.

It noted that while the team did not find any design issue that could lead to a cause of the crashes, "the FAA has concluded that they (the recommendations) address unsafe conditions that must be corrected through the issuance of ADs."
"Therefore," the agency said, "the FAA does not concur that the design changes merely enhanced the (model 737's) already acceptable level of safety."
The changes call for the modification of the plane's rudder power control units to try to prevent contamination by hydraulic fluid that could reduce rudder movement.
The FAA estimated the modifications to cost up to $16,880 per plane and said the design change affected about 2,675 model 737s in the worldwide fleet, about 1,100 of which are flown by U.S. carriers.
The crashes that prompted the design review were in Pittsburgh, in 1994, that killed all 132 people on board, and in Colorado Springs, Colorado, in 1991, that killed 25 people.
